inputs.need:
I am the antimicrobial stewardship pharmacist for a network of three hospitals: a 610-bed teaching hospital and two community hospitals of 180 and 140 beds. Our stewardship team is 2.4 full-time pharmacist equivalents and one infectious diseases physician at 0.3 of a full-time post. For five years we have run prospective audit and feedback on the medical wards of the teaching hospital: a pharmacist reviews every patient on a restricted or broad-spectrum antimicrobial on day 3 and leaves a written recommendation in the chart, and twice a week discusses recommendations in person on a joint round, which we call handshake rounds. Acceptance of recommendations runs at about 71 percent on medicine, but in a six-week surgical try-out last spring it was only 54 percent, and the two community sites have never had more than telephone advice.

Our antimicrobial stewardship committee has to decide, at its meeting in April 2027, whether and how to extend audit and feedback to the surgical wards, the intensive care unit and the two community hospitals, with the same staff. Committee members disagree. Some argue from the numbers: days of therapy, length of therapy, C. difficile, costs. Others argue that the real problem is how surgeons and intensivists receive the feedback, and that remote written advice will simply be ignored.

I would like to do a scoping review that maps both kinds of evidence and keeps them apart. On one side, what has been measured about audit and feedback programmes: antimicrobial use, clinical outcomes, costs, acceptance rates and staffing, especially in surgery, intensive care and small hospitals. On the other side, what is known about how prescribers, pharmacists and nurses experience and act on stewardship recommendations: why they accept or decline, the role of hierarchy and timing, and in-person versus written feedback. I want each side to have its own main question and its own main result, so that the committee sees both without one being forced into the other. I am not looking for a pooled effect size.

Practical points. The network library can run searches in the main bibliographic databases and has agreed to help. One of our pharmacy residents can be a second screener from January, and an infectious diseases fellow has offered to read the experience studies with me. The committee wants a written summary by the end of March 2027, and we have no research budget. Our own audit data are for context only and will not be analysed in the review. Several committee members asked that nurse perspectives be included, because nurses often carry the recommendation to the team after the pharmacist leaves. Reports in French should be included where possible, because one community hospital serves a mostly French-speaking population and some provincial stewardship reports exist only in French.

What I need from the planning is a clear question for each side, a charting approach that keeps them separate, a realistic screening plan for four hours a week plus the resident and the fellow, and an honest statement of what a map of this kind can and cannot tell the committee about extending the service to surgery, intensive care and the small hospitals. The committee also asked whether any report describes extending audit and feedback to new wards without new staff, and what then happened to acceptance on the original wards, because that is exactly our situation.
inputs.constraints: No research budget. Stewardship pharmacist time for the review is limited to four hours a week from October 2026 to March 2027. The pharmacy resident is available as second screener for four hours a week from January 2027 only. The infectious diseases fellow can read experience studies for two hours a week. The committee needs a written summary of no more than four pages plus appendices by 31 March 2027 for its meeting on 14 April 2027. The two strands (measured outcomes, and experience of recommendations) must be charted and reported separately, each with its own main result; no pooled effect size. The network's own audit and feedback data are context only and must not be analysed as part of the review. Reports in English and French are eligible; there is no budget for other translations. No contact with prescribers, nurses or patients for this review. The library can design and run searches but cannot screen or chart. Reports from 2005 onward only. Charting forms for the two strands must be tested on no more than ten reports before full charting begins. Draft findings may be shared with the committee chair once, in the week of 1 March 2027, and must not be circulated further before the meeting.

Days of therapy per 1000 patient-days in 2025 were 612 on the teaching hospital's medical wards and 741 on its surgical wards (network stewardship report, context only).

response.title: Prospective audit and feedback for antimicrobial stewardship: a two-strand scoping review for extending the service
response.subtitle: Measured outcomes and experience of recommendations, charted as separate strands
response.statement: A three-hospital network runs prospective audit and feedback on the teaching hospital's medical wards and must decide in April 2027 whether and how to extend it to surgery, intensive care and two community hospitals with the same staff. Committee members disagree on whether the case rests on measured outcomes or on how prescribers receive feedback. A scoping review will map both kinds of evidence as separate strands, each with its own question and main result, without pooling.
response.whoAffected: Inpatients exposed to unnecessary broad-spectrum antimicrobials, especially in surgery and intensive care; prescribers, pharmacists and nurses who give and receive recommendations; the two community hospitals without on-site stewardship; and the committee.
response.whatHurts: Unnecessary antimicrobial days drive resistance, C. difficile and adverse effects; recommendations that are ignored waste scarce pharmacist time; extending the service badly could spread staff too thin everywhere.
response.currentPractice: Day-3 pharmacist review with written recommendations on medical wards, handshake rounds twice a week on two wards, and telephone advice only for the community hospitals.
response.whyNow: The committee decides in April 2027 and has asked for a written summary by 31 March; the surgical try-out showed low acceptance of written recommendations.
response.constraints: No budget; four pharmacist hours a week to March 2027; second screener from January; fellow two hours a week; summary by 31 March 2027; two strands reported separately; English and French.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Patients in every ward and hospital of the network receive the antimicrobials they need for as long as they need them, and no longer.
response.summary: Problem framed as a two-strand scoping question to inform the extension of audit and feedback.

records.title: Prospective audit and feedback on medical wards and days of antimicrobial therapy: an interrupted time series across four hospitals
records.authors: Ashworth-Mensah R, Delgado-Frye N, Nakashima-Obi L
records.abstract: We introduced prospective audit and feedback by stewardship pharmacists on the medical wards of four hospitals and analysed monthly days of therapy per 1000 patient-days for 24 months before and 24 months after. Days of therapy fell by 11 percent at introduction, with no further trend, and the fall was largest for carbapenems and anti-pseudomonal penicillins. Acceptance of recommendations was 74 percent. Rates of C. difficile infection, 30-day mortality and readmission did not change. Two hospitals changed their empirical guidelines during the study, which may account for part of the fall.

records.title: Handshake stewardship versus remote written review on surgical wards: acceptance of recommendations and antimicrobial use
records.abstract: On six surgical wards of two hospitals, we compared quarters of in-person handshake rounds with quarters of remote written review over 18 months, alternating by quarter. Acceptance was 81 percent with handshake rounds and 52 percent with written review. Days of therapy were 9 percent lower in handshake quarters. Handshake rounds took about 3 more pharmacist hours per ward per week. Surgeons valued discussing the duration of prophylaxis in person. The alternating design reduced but did not remove the influence of secular trends.

records.title: Why surgeons decline stewardship recommendations: a thematic analysis of 38 conversations
records.abstract: We analysed 38 conversations with surgeons and surgical trainees about antimicrobial stewardship recommendations they had declined. Themes included uncertainty about who was responsible for antimicrobial decisions on the team, recommendations arriving after the ward round when plans were fixed, a sense that written notes from pharmacists lacked clinical context, and fear of infection in patients with implants. Recommendations discussed in person and early in the day were described as easier to act on. Participants suggested that the most senior surgeon present should be the named recipient.

records.title: Prescriber experience of audit and feedback in intensive care: hierarchy, timing and trust
records.abstract: We held focus groups with 26 intensivists, trainees and critical care pharmacists in three intensive care units about stewardship feedback. Participants described feedback as welcome when delivered at the daily multidisciplinary round by a pharmacist who was part of the unit team, and as intrusive when it came from outside. Trainees reported that they could not act on recommendations without consultant agreement. Trust built over months of joint rounds, and turnover of pharmacists reset it. Nurses were often the ones who reminded the team of stop dates.

records.title: Mapping outcome measures in antimicrobial stewardship evaluations: a review of 142 studies
records.authors: Thibodeaux-Ansah P, Hollingsworth-Emeka D, Varga-Sato C
records.abstract: We catalogued the outcome measures used in 142 evaluations of hospital stewardship interventions. Days of therapy were reported in 61 percent, defined daily doses in 38 percent and both in 12 percent. Clinical outcomes were reported by 44 percent, most often mortality, and C. difficile by 33 percent. Only 19 percent reported acceptance of recommendations, and 7 percent reported pharmacist time. Denominators differed between patient-days, admissions and days present, which prevents direct comparison. The authors propose days of therapy per 1000 days present as a common measure.

records.title: Clostridioides difficile infection and mortality after stewardship audit and feedback programmes: a pooled analysis of 17 hospitals
records.abstract: We pooled data from 17 hospitals that introduced audit and feedback between 2008 and 2013 and compared the incidence of hospital-onset C. difficile infection and in-hospital mortality in the two years before and after. C. difficile incidence fell by 18 percent, but the fall was concentrated in hospitals that also restricted fluoroquinolones at the same time. In-hospital mortality did not change. Hospitals with fewer than 200 beds contributed 4 of the 17 sites and showed wider variation. The authors caution that concurrent restriction policies make attribution difficult.

records.title: Pharmacist workload and recommendation acceptance in stewardship audit and feedback: a time-and-motion study
records.abstract: We timed stewardship pharmacists' audit and feedback work over 40 weekdays at three hospitals. Reviewing a patient took a median of 7 minutes, writing a recommendation 4 minutes, and an in-person discussion 6 minutes. Pharmacists covering more than 30 patients a day wrote shorter recommendations, and acceptance fell from 76 to 61 percent as daily caseload rose. Community hospital sites had the longest travel and waiting times for in-person discussion. The authors estimate that extending audit and feedback to surgical wards would need about 0.5 additional pharmacist FTE per 100 beds.

records.title: Nurses' role in stewardship feedback rounds: perspectives from ward teams
records.abstract: We held 22 conversations with ward nurses, nurse managers and stewardship pharmacists on medical and surgical wards about how stewardship recommendations are passed on. Nurses described themselves as the link between the pharmacist's note and the team, reminding doctors of review dates and intravenous-to-oral switches. They felt their role was invisible in stewardship reports and that recommendations written only in the chart were often missed. Several suggested that nurses attend handshake rounds when possible. The findings come from two hospitals with established stewardship teams.

records.title: Sustaining audit and feedback after programme funding ends: a five-year follow-up of three hospitals
records.abstract: We followed three hospitals for five years after dedicated funding for audit and feedback ended. Two hospitals kept the service with existing pharmacists but reviewed fewer patients a day, and days of therapy drifted back up by 6 percent over three years. The third hospital stopped audit and feedback and returned to its pre-programme level within 18 months. Sites that kept in-person rounds maintained higher acceptance. The authors suggest planning staffing for the long term before extending programmes to new wards or sites.

response.synthesis: Nine retrieved records, charted at abstract level into two strands. Strand A (measured outcomes): audit and feedback reduced antimicrobial use modestly on medical wards; in surgery, acceptance and use depended on in-person delivery; acceptance fell as caseload rose; clinical outcomes rarely changed and were confounded by concurrent policies; measures and denominators vary. Strand B (experience of recommendations): surgeons and intensivists act on recommendations that arrive on time, in person and from a trusted team member; trainees defer to consultants; nurses carry recommendations to the team but are invisible in reports. As a scoping review, no certainty is assigned to either strand.
response.gradeRationale: Not assessed: a scoping review maps the evidence and does not rate certainty.
response.summary: Nine retrieved records charted into two strands; seven claims; no certainty assigned by design.

response.reading: The committee's disagreement follows the two strands. Measured outcomes show a modest effect on use that depends on delivery and staffing (claims c1, c2, c5) and are reported with incompatible measures (claim c6). Experience evidence explains why: recommendations work when they arrive on time, in person, from a trusted team member, and when nurses carry them (claims c3, c4, c7). Extending written feedback to surgery, intensive care and small hospitals with the same staff is exactly where both strands predict weak acceptance.

response.title: Prospective audit and feedback for antimicrobial stewardship: a two-strand scoping review of measured outcomes and experience of recommendations
response.abstract: Objective: to map measured outcomes of prospective audit and feedback (strand A) and experience of stewardship recommendations (strand B), with attention to surgery, intensive care and small hospitals. Design: scoping review following JBI guidance with a convergent segregated approach, reported with PRISMA-ScR. Results will be charted by March 2027.
response.introduction: Audit and feedback reduces antimicrobial use modestly, but results depend on how recommendations are delivered and received. A stewardship committee needs both kinds of evidence, kept separate, to decide how to extend the service.
response.methods: Searches by the network library; screening by a pharmacist with a second screener from January; strand A charted with 20 percent verification; strand B coded jointly with an infectious diseases fellow; joint display for surgery, intensive care and small hospitals. Certainty was not rated.
response.results: No charting has been done yet. The report will present the PRISMA-ScR flow diagram, the strand A evidence map, the strand B framework synthesis and the joint display.
response.discussion: The discussion will set out what each strand says about extending the service with the same staff and where the evidence is silent.
response.limitations: English and French only; single screening early on; few small-hospital reports.
response.conclusion: To be written after charting; it will describe the evidence and will not estimate effects.
response.summary: PRISMA-ScR draft with results left empty until charting.

store.title: Prospective audit and feedback for antimicrobial stewardship: a two-strand scoping review for extending the service
store.problem.rawNeed:
I am the antimicrobial stewardship pharmacist for a network of three hospitals: a 610-bed teaching hospital and two community hospitals of 180 and 140 beds. Our stewardship team is 2.4 full-time pharmacist equivalents and one infectious diseases physician at 0.3 of a full-time post. For five years we have run prospective audit and feedback on the medical wards of the teaching hospital: a pharmacist reviews every patient on a restricted or broad-spectrum antimicrobial on day 3 and leaves a written recommendation in the chart, and twice a week discusses recommendations in person on a joint round, which we call handshake rounds. Acceptance of recommendations runs at about 71 percent on medicine, but in a six-week surgical try-out last spring it was only 54 percent, and the two community sites have never had more than telephone advice.

Our antimicrobial stewardship committee has to decide, at its meeting in April 2027, whether and how to extend audit and feedback to the surgical wards, the intensive care unit and the two community hospitals, with the same staff. Committee members disagree. Some argue from the numbers: days of therapy, length of therapy, C. difficile, costs. Others argue that the real problem is how surgeons and intensivists receive the feedback, and that remote written advice will simply be ignored.

I would like to do a scoping review that maps both kinds of evidence and keeps them apart. On one side, what has been measured about audit and feedback programmes: antimicrobial use, clinical outcomes, costs, acceptance rates and staffing, especially in surgery, intensive care and small hospitals. On the other side, what is known about how prescribers, pharmacists and nurses experience and act on stewardship recommendations: why they accept or decline, the role of hierarchy and timing, and in-person versus written feedback. I want each side to have its own main question and its own main result, so that the committee sees both without one being forced into the other. I am not looking for a pooled effect size.

Practical points. The network library can run searches in the main bibliographic databases and has agreed to help. One of our pharmacy residents can be a second screener from January, and an infectious diseases fellow has offered to read the experience studies with me. The committee wants a written summary by the end of March 2027, and we have no research budget. Our own audit data are for context only and will not be analysed in the review. Several committee members asked that nurse perspectives be included, because nurses often carry the recommendation to the team after the pharmacist leaves. Reports in French should be included where possible, because one community hospital serves a mostly French-speaking population and some provincial stewardship reports exist only in French.

What I need from the planning is a clear question for each side, a charting approach that keeps them separate, a realistic screening plan for four hours a week plus the resident and the fellow, and an honest statement of what a map of this kind can and cannot tell the committee about extending the service to surgery, intensive care and the small hospitals. The committee also asked whether any report describes extending audit and feedback to new wards without new staff, and what then happened to acceptance on the original wards, because that is exactly our situation.
store.problem.constraints: No research budget. Stewardship pharmacist time for the review is limited to four hours a week from October 2026 to March 2027. The pharmacy resident is available as second screener for four hours a week from January 2027 only. The infectious diseases fellow can read experience studies for two hours a week. The committee needs a written summary of no more than four pages plus appendices by 31 March 2027 for its meeting on 14 April 2027. The two strands (measured outcomes, and experience of recommendations) must be charted and reported separately, each with its own main result; no pooled effect size. The network's own audit and feedback data are context only and must not be analysed as part of the review. Reports in English and French are eligible; there is no budget for other translations. No contact with prescribers, nurses or patients for this review. The library can design and run searches but cannot screen or chart. Reports from 2005 onward only. Charting forms for the two strands must be tested on no more than ten reports before full charting begins. Draft findings may be shared with the committee chair once, in the week of 1 March 2027, and must not be circulated further before the meeting.
